title: Padres' Mason Miller back for Game 4 after brief paternity list stint - CBS Sports
description: Miller imploded in Game 2 of the NLDS against the Brewers, then went on the paternity list and missed Game 3
body:
Miller imploded in Game 2 of the NLDS against the Brewers, then went on the paternity list and missed Game 3
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:32 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Padres closer Mason Miller is back and good to go for Game 4 in San Diego on Wednesday night as his team tries to stave off elimination again. He was reactivated for the game and Wandy Rodriguez was removed, the team announced Wednesday afternoon.Miller was placed on the paternity list prior to Game 3 of the NLDS with the Padres trailing the Brewers 0-2 in the best-of-five series. The Padres were able to pull off the victory in Game 3 with a 4-3 win, which included a two-inning save by starting pitcher Michael King.In Sunday's Game 2, with the Padres clinging to a one-run lead late, Miller failed to pull off his own two-inning save. Instead, the Brewers stormed back and won in walk-off fashion to take the 2-0 series lead. Miller recorded outs vs. the first four hitters he faced, but then walked three of the next four hitters he saw and gave up a two-RBI single to Jackson Chourio to take the blown save and loss. Entering Game 4, Miller is now on three days of rest. He came into the playoffs as arguably the best closer in baseball, racking up 38 saves and a 1.67 ERA in the regular season.
Meanwhile, lefty Adrián Morejón, the Padres' second-biggest late-inning gun, hasn't pitched since going two innings in Game 1. It made sense that he didn't pitch in Game 2, but he wasn't available in Game 3 either, due to a previously undisclosed shoulder issue. Stammen said on Wednesday that he's "hopeful" Morejón will be available."Still feeling a little stickiness in the shoulder," Stammen said after Game 3. "We're trying to work through it. We're doing everything we can to get him ready. We'll see his status about tomorrow, but he was definitely feeling a little bit better today but just didn't feel like he could go."There's definitely a chance [he pitches in Game 4], yeah. We'll see. We've got to evaluate him [Wednesday] like we did today and put him in a safe space to be able to pitch. We don't want to put him out there if he's compromised."
The Padres still have excellent relievers like Jason Adam and Bradgley Rodriguez, but the bullpen is a monster force when the best versions of Miller and Morejón are 100%. Perhaps we'll find out in Game 4 if that's the case.

title: Why Dana Altman followed Bruce Pearl, Tony Bennett's footsteps with sudden retirement on eve of 2026-27 season - CBS Sports
description: There's a common thread that connects the recent string of last-second retirements in college basketball
body:
There's a common thread that connects the recent string of last-second retirements in college basketball
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    3:24 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            4 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        It happened again.For the third straight season, a longtime sitting head coach has retired just weeks before the season opener. Oregon's Dana Altman -- the best coach in program history -- retired effective immediately Wednesday, less than 24 hours before the 68-year-old was slated to take the podium at Big Ten Media Days in Chicago.Virginia's Tony Bennett in 2024. Auburn's Bruce Pearl in 2025. Now, Altman follows suit in flying away from the Ducks in 2026.The common grumbles about NIL (excuse me, pay-for-play) and the portal (excuse me, free agency) are staples of the conversation, like usual. Altman grew frustrated with the consistent roster turnover and the voluminous court orders, injunctions and temporary restraining orders that have exploded after the NCAA's poorly timed rollout of the new five-in-five eligibility model, sources told CBS Sports. Altman had taken a backseat in portal negotiations this spring, handing the baton to top assistant Tony Stubblefield, who is now Oregon's interim head coach. Altman being swirled with retirement murmurs was nothing new.But let's call a spade a spade: Bennett, Pearl and now Altman all bid adieu to rosters that left much to be desired. Bennett's last Virginia squad rated 80th nationally on kenpom.com in the preseason. Virginia would go on to finish just 15-17 and outside the top 100 nationally for the first time since 2010-11. Pearl was fresh off leading Auburn to the 2025 Final Four, but he had to replace seven of the top eight players on the roster, including All-American Johni Broome and multiple other NBA players in Dylan Cardwell, Miles Kelly and Chaney Johnson. Pearl helped construct a roster that rated outside the top 30 nationally in the preseason, and sure enough, it finished 36th and on the outside looking in for the Big Dance. Handing his son, Steven, the head coaching job was certainly part of Bruce Pearl's calculus for retirement, but I'd be hard-pressed to believe Pearl would've had the stomach to simply walk away from another national championship contender. That dude loved to be in the fight. 

        
            
                Big Ten expert picks: Projected order of finish, preseason predictions, top players to watch, starting lineups
                
                    Isaac Trotter                
            
                            
    
                
                    
    
A similar script is being emulated in Eugene. Preseason prognostications aren't gospel after the whackiest offseason in college basketball history, but Evan Miya tabbed Oregon at 56th nationally in his early projections, and the Ducks were picked 13th in CBS Sports' Big Ten preview. It's hard to argue with those grim outlooks when you look at a roster featuring major questions at the two most important positions on the floor: point guard and center. The PG1 was supposed to be Jackson Shelstad, who grew up in West Linn, Oregon, and idolized legendary Ducks guard Payton Pritchard. But Shelstad made the tough decision to leave. He transferred to Louisville this spring for a reported $4 million payday. That left a sting on Altman. This roster looks far different (and better) if Shelstad had stuck around for his senior season.The stereotype that Oregon had no money frankly doesn't apply here, either. Even though close to $50 million has been dumped into building the Ducks' football roster, Oregon's coffers weren't fully empty for hoops. Oregon had north of $12 million to build a basketball roster. That's not elite money in the Big Ten, where Michigan, Indiana and Illinois are humming at $20 million or above, but it's right in the middle of the pack for a middle-of-the-pack program that was capable of finishing 25-10 in 2024-25 when lots went right and 12-20 in 2025-26 when injuries riddled the roster.
Altman finishes his career just eight wins away from the 800 Club. No rival coach will miss seeing Altman on the sidelines in the NCAA Tournament, where his teams seemed to play their best ball. He went 17-9 in the Big Dance at Oregon. A pretty good ledger in the most unpredictable tournament sports has to offer.What now for Oregon's current players?The timing of Altman's decision is by design and likely keeps Oregon's players from entering the transfer portal. By elevating Stubblefield to interim head coach status, Oregon's players cannot enter the transfer portal for 31 days -- not until Nov. 7. This rule was put in place to give the interim coach the time and opportunity to retain players.Altman knows that the timing of this keeps the players locked into the Oregon roster, unless they want to risk missing the whole year to transfer and redshirt. 
It also makes more sense, financially, for these players to stay in Eugene for the 2026-27 season. While it's a bit rude to the players who committed to play for Altman, it's not a total kneecapping. The direct deposits will still keep cashing. Oregon's entire staff will get paid for another year. Oregon's brass also knew this day was coming. It will have a head start to sniff around top candidates before next spring's carousel. A mid-major hotshot like New Mexico's Eric Olen would make sense, but Oregon has the resources to make a strong impression on a high-major coach who wants access to that sweet, sweet Nike money. There's always something under the surface for decisions this abrupt. It just so happens that this is the third time a last-second heel-turn occurs when the roster isn't elite.
It isn't a coincidence.

title: 2026 MLB playoffs: Winners and losers as Guardians stave off elimination vs. White Sox - CBS Sports
description: The White Sox stacked up missed opportunities in Game 3 and allowed Cleveland to force a Game 4 on Thursday
body:
The White Sox stacked up missed opportunities in Game 3 and allowed Cleveland to force a Game 4 on Thursday
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    7:25 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        MLB's postseason continued Wednesday with four potential Division Series clinchers. Regardless of the outcomes, this will be the last day with four games this season, so enjoy it. We won't get more than two games per day moving forward.On the American League side, the Chicago White Sox and Tampa Bay Rays are trying to finish three-game sweeps over the Cleveland Guardians and New York Yankees, respectively. In the National League, the Los Angeles Dodgers and Milwaukee Brewers will try to close out their series with the Atlanta Braves and San Diego Padres, again respectively, in Game 4.Here are the final scores and schedule for Wednesday's postseason action:FINAL: Guardians 9, White Sox 3 (box score); White Sox lead series 2-1LIVE: Dodgers at Braves (box score); Dodgers lead series 2-1UPCOMING: Rays at Yankees (GameTracker); Rays lead series 2-0UPCOMING: Brewers at Padres (GameTracker); Brewers lead series 2-1To sum up all the Division Series action, we're here to declare a winner and loser from each of the four Wednesday contests. You can find those declarations just below. 
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Winner: Jo AdellThe Guardians acquired Adell in front of the trade deadline and he's been an RBI machineAs the trade deadline came into focus, the Guardians, looking for cheap help on offense, ended up grabbing outfielder Jo Adell from the Angels in exchange for Double-A catcher Jacob Cozart. In 48 games for Cleveland, Adell posted a 108 OPS+ and drove home 32 runs. In Game 2, he recorded an eighth-inning RBI triple that nearly left the yard.
In Game 3 on Wednesday in Game 3, he came to the plate with two outs, bases loaded and a tied 1-1 score. Adell came through in a big way. Just like that, it was a 4-1 Guardians lead. Adell also became the 16th player in postseason history to triple in back-to-back games (via Sarah Langs). Adell's three-RBI triple moved the Guardians' chances to win the game from 52.8% to 78.8%. This was the largest difference-maker in the game, and a monster shift at that.
                            
    
                                                
                    
    Loser: White Sox's missed opportunitiesThe White Sox had plenty of chances for crooked numbers in this onePlaying in front of an electric crowd, ready to clinch a postseason series at home for the first time since 1906 (and we all remember that one, right?), the White Sox had several chances to put up a crooked number and weren't able to come through. 
In the first, Sam Anonacci walked and Miguel Vargas singled to give them two runners with no outs. Kyle Teel came through with a one-out double, but Vargas was held at third. Chase Meidroth and Tristan Peters struck out to leave two on base.Meidroth and Peters started the fourth with consecutive doubles, but the following three hitters were retired, so, again, the White Sox settled for just the one run.In the fifth, Antonacci singled and Vargas walked. The runners moved up on a grounder and then Teel ripped a line drive toward right field, only to watch it get snared by Guardians second baseman Travis Bazzana, who then doubled Vargas off second. The expected batting average on this one makes it even tougher to swallow for the White Sox faithful, as it was .940. This means that 94% of the time a ball hit with that exit velocity at that launch angle ends up as a hit. This was one of the 6% that found a glove. In the sixth, with two outs, Braden Montgomery walked, Randal Grichuk singled, Colson Montgomery was hit by a pitch and then so was Antonacci. They got a run, but the bases were loaded for their best player, Vargas. He hit a rocket toward left, but Guardians third baseman José Ramírez was able to knock the ball down and get Vargas at first. Vargas hit it hard, with a .580 expected batting average. It just didn't work out. You never want to come away empty-handed in those innings, and the White Sox were able to get a single run in three of those frames. Still, it feels like there was a lot left on the board here from the home team. An explosion in a single inning could've demoralized the Guardians and ultimately sent them home. Some of the issues were their own fault, and some were bad luck. It all added up to a Game 4 White Sox loss.

title: Change in Houston: DeMeco Ryans taking over defensive play-calling duties from Matt Burke - CBS Sports
description: Burke had called plays since early last season
body:
Burke had called plays since early last season
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:48 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            2 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        On Wednesday, Houston Texans coach DeMeco Ryans said he will take over defensive play-calling duties from defensive coordinator Matt Burke, a significant change amid his team's 0-4 start."It all starts with me," Ryans said. "If there's a lack in communication, I look at myself first, so it starts with me and making sure I'm a better communicator, so just to help spark things more, I'm gonna take over the play calling for the defense, and I'm gonna make sure the communication is right. If our guys are saying the communication is not right, then ... ultimately it falls on me. So it's on me to get it fixed."It's no slight against coach Burke. He's done an outstanding job. Just wanna make sure I can streamline communication in the best way possible, so that isn't the theme when I stand up here the next time I see you guys and talking about communication."The change comes on the heels of Houston's 34-30 loss to the Dallas Cowboys in which Dallas racked up 399 yards of offense and scored touchdowns on four of its five second-half drives. CeeDee Lamb had 17 catches for 189 yards and a touchdown, and Dak Prescott threw for 335 yards. Dallas did not have a single turnover.It was the second time in four weeks that the defense was not up to its usual excellent standard. The Bills beat the Texans 36-31 in Week 1. Houston still ranks highly in many categories, but one notable drop-off has been in the number of big plays it is giving up.
Texans' defensive ranks20252026Success rate2nd8thSack rate8th3rdNet yards per attempt4th25thExplosive play rate14th28thThe Texans' defense gives up some big plays by nature -- it is an extremely aggressive unit that will sometimes get beaten -- but the fall from 14th to 28th in explosive play rate is massive. Several big plays have also come in crucial moments, magnifying the problem even more.In Week 1, Josh Allen threw a game-winning 34-yard touchdown pass to Joshua Palmer with under a minute left.In Week 3, Daniel Jones found Laquon Treadwell for 20 yards with under two minutes left before the game-winning field goal.In Week 4, Prescott found George Pickens for 22 yards with under a minute left shortly before the game-winning touchdown.The Texans have allowed 17 completions of 20+ yards. Only the Lions have allowed more. There is much more to "communication" than just defending big plays -- many of those completions were well-defended -- but that is one area in which Houston is lacking.Last year, Ryans gave up play-calling duties to Burke in Week 4, ironically, after the Texans' defense had been struggling early. Ryans is now hoping the inverse decision from last year will provide a similar spark.
The Texans started 1-3 last season and made the playoffs. Only one team -- the 1992 Chargers -- started a season 0-4 and made the postseason. The Texans will hope their march to join them starts with a win in Week 5 at the Titans.

title: How USWNT coach Emma Hayes is rebuilding U.S. Soccer's women's program ahead of World Cup - CBS Sports
description: ATLANTA -- When Emma Hayes took the job as U.S. women's national team manager in 2024, she took it head-on, knowing the clock was tickin
body:
ATLANTA -- When Emma Hayes took the job as U.S. women's national team manager in 2024, she took it head-on, knowing the clock was ticking toward the 2024 Summer Olympics. She and the USWNT achieved quick success and made history by returning to the top of the Olympic podium for the first time since 2012, with roughly 80 days officially on the job. After the gold medal win, and between planning for the 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup and the 2028 Olympics, Hayes has done more than coach players; she has built an ecosystem dedicated to the growth, support, and development of women and young girls in soccer. This isn't exactly breaking news. Hayes has been vocal about her broader ambitions in her current role to push the game forward. She launched the strategy "The WNT Way" in 2025, a vision that began by centering women at the heart of all processes in U.S. Soccer and beyond. Before the USWNT gathered for training camps ahead of friendlies against Spain, Hayes and U.S. Soccer co-hosted the 2026 herLENS conference, a two-day event highlighting the work already underway with sessions on research and data. Whenever building culture, part of that is through developing and educating the principles, and in the second edition of the conference, Hayes and other session speakers did just that, and spoke with media about the importance of normalizing goals and processes through the lens of a woman. 
"I know that the legacy of the WNT, the impact of the WNT, the importance of the WNT to everyone across this country goes beyond just the team that wins on the field and winning gold medals and winning World Cups, because of course, winning is an important part of the culture," Hayes said in her remarks at the conference."But as far as I'm concerned, winning is about creating a world so that by the time we get to four, five years down the road in 2031 ... That we have not only just reimagined that world, but we've built it collectively, so that everyone across the landscape is in a better position."U.S. Soccer and Hayes aligned beyond 2028A familiar theme over the second edition of the conference was Hayes and her staff's forward-thinking approach. Everyone is tapped into the "Female 360" approach, which includes plenty of player surveying, one-on-ones, and individual programs for each athlete, including overall health check-ins from hydration to nutrition strategies and menstrual cycle tracking to help players improve performance and overall health.
While Hayes was vocal in 2025 about building and implementing women-focused research and support for athletes, it's been a bigger vision with her since her days with Chelsea. She points to the 2016 FA Cup final loss with Chelsea, a 1-0 defeat against rivals Arsenal at Wembley Stadium, as a turning point that drove her toward a more women-centered approach to game prep and individual player planning. She noted the players' slower reaction time and coordination that day and that it looked like she was watching a group of people separated from their bodies. "I remember at the end of the game, one of my staff saying, 'You know, we have the vast majority of our players are in phase four, beginning of phase one.' I was like, 'What does that mean? And then I, honestly, my own, like, awakening was, I don't even think I understand my own period,'" Hayes quipped.Phase four refers to menstrual cycle tracking, and it isn't unique to the Hayes era of the USWNT. It was a significant part of the team's preparations for the 2019 FIFA Women's World Cup, led by former performance coach and sports scientist Dawn Scott. It's one mechanism U.S. Soccer is building on in the Hayes era, as the coach pushes for more development in women's coaching and leadership positions and investments in sports medicine, and is also trying to think beyond winning.
Hayes has been open and transparent about her previous battles with stage five endometriosis, all in an effort to help normalize the conversation around it and to potentially help others in the long run. "We can only do it as a collective. That's what I realized. Using it as a competitive advantage when I was at Chelsea is one thing. Using it as a competitive advantage when the U.S. Women's National Team, yeah, there are things that I definitely won't reveal because I want to win. But I want every little girl and woman, no matter what your practice is in our sport, to feel like, I don't know, this is more than just playing the game. I actually think we can impact society in a profound way."Emma Hayes' presence a key factorBetween planning for competitions, it's been about setting up the program and its youth teams for future, sustainable success. From planning "futures camps" to reestablishing the U23 program to being a vocal advocate for the U20 team's tournaments, Hayes is making sure that, no matter what, coaches, staff, and leaders in the space work toward the same goal, centering all processes on women. 
It's a simple concept: take processes and protocols that have already been copied and pasted from the men's game to the women's game -- smash them, and rebuild and reimagine them specifically for women and girls. It sounds far simpler than it actually is, as support and resources for the women's game are decades behind what has been built for men. Eighteen months after launching the WNT Way, direct support for players through the "Female 360" approach remains in full effect, adding new layers like a bigger herLENS conference in year two and a strategic partnership with Kang Women's Institute for the herLENS Research Consortium. The partnership will focus on key questions in women's and girls' soccer, from how performance data is collected and used to why girls step away from the game.Creating the environment has gone beyond a 2027 cycle, as the World Cup is now just eight months away, with the 2028 Olympics set to follow. The U.S. Soccer Federation is expected to host the 2031 World Cup alongside CONCACAF partners Mexico, Costa Rica, and Jamaica, and discussions around a longstanding female-centric ecosystem led by Hayes are spoken of as the normal long term, though her initial managerial contract was announced through 2027.
"This was always the plan from the beginning. When we hired Emma, it was about six months until she started, and we knew she was going to be coming in right before the Olympics. And I always said, this is not a short-term thing. Like we want to win the Olympics, but we want someone who's going to lead our federation on the women and girls side for a long period of time," said U.S. Soccer president Cindy Parlow Cone."So, this has always been in the plan. And so, if you only look at the cycle now, you're not developing for the future and putting things into place more long term. So if you scan out and say, 'Okay, where do we want to be in '31?  Okay, if that's where we want to be, where do we want to be in '27 and '28? How do we build towards that? So Emma has my full support. I'm like the plow in front of her, making sure she's got a clear runway."Building into the World CupThe biggest difference for Hayes and her staff implementing and operating in their Female 360 approach now versus when she first arrived is time. Hayes had from June until reaching the top of the Olympic podium to troubleshoot some of her approaches. She retells a funny story about realizing the short window of time and what she and her staff could realistically achieve between her arrival and August 10—the day of the Olympic final. 
"I always go back to what's the most important things: sleep and food. Okay, how can we not f--- that up? You've got to get sleep right. You've got to get nutrition right. When you've got so many male-lens approaches to things like traditional performances, we put weighing scales outside the room, or the meal prep will be exactly the same. I'll be like, 'Do you realize the stress levels that's going on for that athlete as she comes in here knowing she's going to be weighed in and it could be moving in a direction that's going to impact her whole day?' And that might be like that because her period is coming? And she's got a bit more water retention, and she's got a bit more inflammation? She might already have the overthinking that's going on. Now I've got to coach that player."Hayes goes on with her example that depending on the player, they might be self-conscious about the scale and therefore second-guess her nutrition throughout the day. She recalls being in France, and the plate sizes of the hotel being smaller and how that alone could affect a player's serving size as they approach the meal room to serve themselves. "They're not going to fill the small plates. If the plate looks small, they're going to put half an amount on that. So something as simple as changing the plates, so we get the right amount ... But you kick that scale out of the way. You don't make everything about data, data, data. You ask. You see. You build that connection," Hayes explained.
"That's what we're doing. Because that's what a traditional performance lens has been. If I'm looking to volleyball, I'm looking to basketball on the women's side. I'm looking for innovation to be able to do it better. But what I found most useful is -- listen to the players; they'll tell you. But only if they're not in a situation where it's feeling like you're gathering data for data's sake, or there's judgment because maybe they don't, you know, want to do something. I'm very much about, like, you have to meet the individual where they are, and they are all very different."In 2025 alone, Hayes used 44 different players in lineups, the most of any coach in the 40-year history of the USWNT program. In her first 32 matches, 32 different players earned first caps, and 60 different players have taken the pitch since she took over. The 26-player roster she named for the October friendlies already has some adjustments to it, with defender Naomi Girma and midfielder Sam Coffey now unavailable for selection due to injuries.Hayes has mentioned that less experienced players are unlikely to start against Spain in the upcoming matches, though she expects them to be ready when called upon. Jaelin Howell and Kate Del Fava have already been called in as replacements, as the U23 squad, which features all active NWSL players, will face the Dominican Republic.
What's nextThe U.S. women's national team will take on Spain in a two-game series beginning Saturday, October 10. The matchup is one of the most anticipated sets of friendlies between the No. 1 and No. 2 teams in the world. The team is currently training at the national training center in Atlanta before heading to Philadelphia for the first match, then to Washington, D.C., to close out the international window on October 13.

title: USWNT's friendlies a chance to ask unanswered questions as World Cup approaches - CBS Sports
description: The USWNT will face Spain in a pair of friendlies that will likely serve as the stiffest test for either team on
body:
The USWNT will face Spain in a pair of friendlies that will likely serve as the stiffest test for either team on the road to next summer's Women's World Cup
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    6:10 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            5 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        A week before the U.S. women's national team opened camp for this month's friendlies against Spain, Emma Hayes spoke about the team's DNA. The four-time world champions are historically one of the game's elite counter-attacking sides; no matter the team's composition on the pitch or in the dugout, the players near the opposition goal always pull focus. That will not change in their back-to-back games against Spain, either, but a more pressing question awaits.How exactly will the USWNT's understaffed defense cope with Spain's attack-oriented DNA?Spain rank amongst the stiffest tests that await any team, such is the natural quality of a reigning World Cup-winning side, but also mark an outlier on the USWNT's schedule following the 2024 Olympics, when Hayes' work revamping the team truly began. Since winning Olympic gold in Paris weeks into Hayes' tenure, the U.S. team have conceded just 15 goals in 34 games and only average seven shots against per match, while their opponents have mustered up an average of just two shots on goal per game. It is not just that they outscore the opposition, no matter the challenger – the USWNT's back line has only had so much to do over the last two years. Spain will reveal whether or not it comes down to the hosts' ability to smother the opposition's attack or whether or not they have even had a chance to prove their worth yet.USWNT schedule against SpainAll times U.S./EasternOct. 10: USWNT vs. Spain, 2:30 p.m. (TBS)Oct. 13: USWNT vs. Spain, 7 p.m. (TNT)Much as she has with her wide-ranging attacking options, Hayes has spent the last two years rotating through her defensive options with the specific intent of building the player pool. Naomi Girma, who rightfully inherited Becky Sauerbrunn's spot at center back before the 2023 Women's World Cup, remains top choice and continues to live up to Hayes' billing as the best defender she's ever worked with. There's just one problem, though – Girma will be unavailable with the re-emergence of a calf injury, which has led Hayes to call on Chelsea to reevaluate their practices.
"This has happened too often and if we want her to be in a position to play games on a regular basis for club and country, I think we have to change some things," Hayes said Tuesday. "She's the last person who wants to be in this place, and she's worked really hard to get herself back to a good level. Obviously I'm not in control of that. I'm not the club. But we are working closely with Chelsea to think differently about creating the right solutions because the player suffers. And I know she's absolutely devastated."There's another issue, too – Gotham FC's Emily Sonnett has often slotted into the back line, the veteran always a solid presence when called upon. She ruptured her patellar tendon in her left knee in July, though, an injury that ruled her out of the remainder of the NWSL season and one that could ultimately jeopardize her chances of playing at a third World Cup. Hayes is down to four options: Sonnett's club and country teammate Tierna Davidson, who started alongside Girma at the Olympics and is the presumptive starter in Brazil; the Washington Spirit's Tara Rudd, one of the early beneficiaries of Hayes' post-Olympics experimentation; the San Diego Wave's Kennedy Wesley, who has just seven caps; and the Utah Royals' Kate Del Fava, a respected NWSL veteran who could earn her first cap at the age of 28.Davidson is the only one of the group with experience playing in major international competitions but perhaps more importantly, none of them have played a full half alongside each other. Davidson and Rudd at least have experience with the national team's rigors under Hayes' leadership, the center back conundrum alone enough to throw a wrench in her plans to play a full-strength lineup for both friendlies against Spain.
The USWNT may not have added cover at defensive midfielder, either. Olympics starter Sam Coffey will also miss the Spain friendlies with an injury she sustained over the weekend with Manchester City, Hayes losing her usual first choice in the process. Bay FC's Claire Hutton was a rival for Coffey's starting spot before the injury and may have earned the nod against Spain regardless but again, this is not a position where the USWNT is necessarily deep. Gotham's Jaelin Howell replaced Coffey on the roster and boasts just six caps, while captain Lindsey Heaps can play there in a pinch but the demands do not match her natural skillset. Hutton boasts plenty of promise on her own, the 20-year-old already poised to be a mainstay on the national team for years to come.Spain is a tough enough challenge but for Hutton in particular, the USWNT's absences at center back mean the strength of the team's spine might rest solely on the midfielder's performances against the world champions.Wrapped up in the questions of the USWNT's spine is how the team will prepare for Spain's well-documented stylistic preferences, specifically their desire to dominate possession. The U.S. team's schedule post-Olympics has offered them a variety of tests, including games against teams that pose physical challenges they have previously been ill-equipped for, but Spain is another test entirely. The USWNT usually dictate the tempo of the game but it is unclear if they will try to nick the ball off the visitors or simply cede possession to Spain, hoping to keep them out other ways. Hutton will likely play a key role in executing the strategy Hayes selects, whichever it may be.
Perhaps above all, though, Hayes' reputation as a tactical pragmatist could be tested over the course of the next week. The injuries to Girma, Coffey and Sonnett are obviously not her fault and her prudent player pool expansion project in the last two years will only lend a helping hand as she figures out how to outdo Spain. The mistakes will not exactly be costly – long before she took this job, the USWNT had used losses in the build-up to major tournaments to identify mistakes that allowed them to go on and collect winners' medals and the upcoming games could serve the same function, regardless of result. In the ultimate bellwether of both teams' ability to win another World Cup in Brazil, though, every decision could very well be a revealing one.

title: Oregon QB Dante Moore unlikely to play vs. UCLA: Dylan Raiola nears first Ducks start - CBS Sports
description: Sources tell CBS Sports the Ducks will likely roll with Raiola against the Bruins as Moore continues his recovery
body:
Sources tell CBS Sports the Ducks will likely roll with Raiola against the Bruins as Moore continues his recovery from a concussion
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    4:12 pm ET

            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        Despite returning to practice this week, Oregon quarterback Dante Moore is "unlikely to play" against UCLA on Saturday, sources tell CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz.On Monday, Ducks coach Dan Lanning said that Moore was back at practice in shoulder pads and a helmet, but the team is taking things slowly with its star quarterback. Oregon will release its first availability report of the week on Wednesday night, but it sounds like Moore will be listed as questionable at best."Dante was out there at practice for us today," Lanning said at his weekly press conference. "Similar to what we said before, we're gonna do what's best for Dante moving forward. ... It was great to see him back out there with his teammates getting to work today."Moore has been recovering from a concussion since taking a dangerous hit to the head against USC on Sept. 26. Trojans linebacker Desman Stephens Jr. struck a forceful blow to Moore's head as he was sliding, and the Oregon quarterback had to be stretchered off the field.
The NCAA's return-to-play protocol for players in the concussion protocol features five stages.Stage 1: Symptom-limited activity: Begin with light aerobic exercise.Stage 2: Moderate aerobic exercise: Increase the intensity of the aerobic exercise.Stage 3: Non-contact drills: Introduce sport-specific drills in full uniform without physical contact.Stage 4: Full-contact practice: Allow full-contact practice or training.Stage 5: Return to competition: An athlete can return to game play only after successfully completing all prior stages and receiving medical clearance.Given that Moore is back at practice, it would be fair to assume he's at least reached Stage 3, but how his body responds to ramping up at practice will be critical for his return timeline.This news means backup Dylan Raiola will likely get his first start at Oregon against UCLA. A former five-star recruit, Raiola transferred from Nebraska in the offseason, and his willingness to play the role of backup for one season is already benefiting him and the Ducks.
In relief of Moore, Raiola torched the USC secondary for 289 yards and a pair of touchdowns. He may need a similar effort this weekend as Oregon faces a UCLA team that has been lighting up the scoreboard under first-year coach Bob Chesney.Confidence in RaiolaRaiola played extremely well in relief of Moore a couple of weeks ago, but it will be his show from the first snap of the game on Saturday. Does being the starter require a shift in mindset for Raiola? Lanning doesn't think so."No, there isn't a shift," Lanning said on Monday. "If he can just play like he played last time every single time, I think we'd be sitting in a really good situation. Dylan's got to keep doing what he's been doing, preparing like he's going to be the guy who goes out there every single day. We need that from every single person on our team. We don't need anything special from Dylan other than doing what he's been doing."
Lanning added that Raiola has shown tremendous accuracy on the practice field, and that showed up on the field against the Trojans. If that keeps up, the Ducks' offense should be just fine."I think all those things show up," Lanning said. "He can play quarterback at a high level. I think he showed his accuracy in this last game and his decision-making. That's shown up for him, and it's shown up for him in practice. Again, I would just ask him to keep doing the same things he's been doing in practice."Among backup quarterbacks around the country, Raiola has a strong case for being the best. How many teams can bring in a player with 24 games of experience, 5,232 passing yards and 36 touchdowns off the bench?
Raiola shouldn't be shaken by the moment in a key top-25 matchup on Saturday afternoon (3:30 p.m. ET, CBS, Paramount+Premium).

title: Why Cowboys have allowed blocked field goals in back-to-back games - CBS Sports
description: Texans coach DeMeco Ryans revealed how Houston copied Baltimore's plan to exploit the same weakness
body:
Texans coach DeMeco Ryans revealed how Houston copied Baltimore's plan to exploit the same weakness
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026

    3:51 pm ET

        With a game on Thursday night, the Dallas Cowboys aren't going to have a lot of practice time, but when they do hit the practice field, they'd better make sure to spend some serious time working on special teams. The Cowboys apparently have a serious flaw in that phase of the game that their opponents have taken advantage of in each of the past two weeks. The flaw involves the Cowboys' field goal team, which has allowed two blocked kicks since Week 3. The first one game in Brazil when the Baltimore Ravens blocked a 59-yard field goal attempt by Brandon Aubrey. 
It was a crucial block because the Cowboys ended up losing by three, 34-31. The second blocked kick came in Week 4, and this time, it was the Texans who blocked Aubrey's field goal try.
That block didn't sting as much because the Cowboys ended up winning 34-30, but it took some last-minute heroics from Dak Prescott and CeeDee Lamb to pull out the victory. 
Having one kicked block is an unfortunate accident, but when you have to two kicks blocked, that's a problem that needs to be immediately addressed. Through four weeks, there have only been six blocked field goal attempts in the NFL all year, so it's definitely an issue if one team has surrendered two of them. Sometimes, when you attempt longer field goals, the kicker will hit the ball at a lower trajectory to add distance, but that's not what happened here as Jerry Jones pointed out during a radio interview with 105.3 The Fan this week. "The problem isn't with the kicker, it's with the protection there," Jones said. "We can fix that. I was shocked, though, that it happened two weeks in a row. That doesn't happen very often because you have a chance to really pointedly work on that."
So why has the Cowboys' field goal team been struggling so much? Houston coach DeMeco Ryans actually answered that exact question during an interview with the Texans' radio team this week. "During the film study, you definitely saw a breakdown in the protection," Ryans said, via PFT. "You've seen it consistently. That's how you study film. You look for those weaknesses, how you can exploit a team. We saw a weakness there in the C and D gap area."When you overwhelm one side of the line, the Cowboys seem unsure who to block. In Houston's situation, the Texans' plan created an opening for Will Anderson, who basically went untouched up the middle to block the kick. A defender should absolutely never be able to penetrate like Anderson did up the middle on a field goal attempt. 
Ryans' coaching staff watched film of what the Ravens did in Week 3. Their plan was to test the Cowboys and exploit the same weakness that Baltimore exploited. "We were able to show that kick from the Baltimore game, how they were able to block it, and we're gonna design a plan similar to that to see if they fixed it," Ryans said. "That's what all teams do. If you see a breakdown, see if they fixed it the next week."The Cowboys clearly didn't fix it. On the block in the Baltimore game, it was on the opposite side, but it was a situation where a defender (Keondre Jackson) came in untouched. Jackson found a huge gap between Terence Steele (78) and Drew Shelton (67). 
Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer admitted that things need to be better. Not to mention, Shelton hasn't practiced this week due to a hamstring injury, so the field goal team could have a new look come Thursday night. "Yeah, moving some pieces around," Schottenheimer said of his field goal team this week. "We were going to move some pieces around anyways because it hasn't been very good. We've got a good rotation going, but at the end of the day, we just got to clean some things up from a technical standpoint."Heading into this week's game against the Buccaneers, the pressure is now on Cowboys special teams coach Nick Sorensen to make sure these problems have been fixed. 
Blocked field goals are rare, but we could see one on Thursday night. Since the start of the 2025 season, Buccaneers kicker Chase McLaughlin has had more field goal attempts blocked (3) than any other kicker. Thanks to the past two weeks, Aubrey is now tied for second on that list with two field goals blocked in that same span.

        It seems like the entire world will be descending upon Tuscaloosa this weekend, including Tropical Storm Isaias. The storm -- which is expected to bring heavy rains and possible flooding -- could impact this weekend's marquee showdown between No. 2 Georgia and No. 6 Alabama.Despite speculation that the storm could move the game to a different day or location, the Crimson Tide and Bulldogs plan on playing in Bryant-Denny Stadium this Saturday, CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz reports. It's possible the kickoff time could shift, but the current plan is to play as scheduled.Earlier this week, an SEC spokesperson told CBS Sports that the conference is "keeping an eye on forecasts and staying in communication with schools with games that could be impacted by weather."The storm is expected to bring locally heavy rain, potential flooding and high winds throughout the Southeast this weekend, although the exact path and timing is unknown. With that in mind, Alabama released a statement on Tuesday saying that there are currently "no plans to alter the contest."
As things stand at the moment, the forecast is calling for a good deal of rain and wind in Tuscaloosa on Saturday, but the conditions could be playable.Current forecast for Alabama vs. GeorgiaTemperature: 69 degreesChance of precipitation: 90 percent chance of rainPrecipitation amount: 1.19 inWind: 20 mph with gusts reaching 38 mphVisibility: 5 miForecast via AccuweatherWhat Kalen DeBoer, Kirby Smart are sayingDuring their SEC teleconference, Alabama coach Kalen DeBoer and Georgia coach Kirby Smart both addressed the possibility of Tropical Storm Isaias affecting the game.Smart said it's hard to simulate tropical storm conditions in practice. Neither Georgia nor Alabama can import a special effects department from Hollywood to create a monsoon on the practice field, but players can learn from how teams have managed messy conditions in the past.
"It's uncertainty. [It's] beyond my control," Smart said, per 247Sports. "We as coaches game plan for multiple situations - weather conditions - when they're there. We had that same prep last week with the threat of those things. Doesn't change a lot about practice. You have to practice good on good. You've got to practice for the long term of the season, not just for one week."You can't really practice conditions. You can't simulate them, so you're much better off to educate, learn from the past of other people who have played in them, and prepare your team to play and not make it about that."DeBoer shared Smart's sentiment, saying there's little that can be done other than preparing as usual. The Crimson Tide will implement wet-ball drills for the second week in a row after prepping for rainy conditions ahead of last weekend's win over Mississippi State.
"Depends on the level of weather you get, it would affect what happens," DeBoer said, according to 247Sports. "It's just -- that's not my area of expertise. I'm just getting our football team ready. It hasn't affected us much, other than we're doing wet ball drills and get wet ball involved in some of our team reps, just like we did last week at times, preparing for the rain a week ago. I'm not really involved in too much."

title: South Carolina's Dylan Stewart on track to play vs. Florida after one-game suspension - CBS Sports
description: Stewart was suspended for one game by the SEC and 'indefinitely' by coach Shane Beamer after punching an Alabama
body:
Stewart was suspended for one game by the SEC and 'indefinitely' by coach Shane Beamer after punching an Alabama player on Sept. 26
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:22 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            3 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        South Carolina EDGE Dylan Stewart is on track to play this Saturday if things continue to progress in the correct direction, CBS Sports' Chris Hummer and Matt Zenitz report.Stewart returned to team activities on Monday after serving a one-game suspension from the SEC for striking an Alabama player in the Gamecocks' loss to the Crimson Tide. In addition to punishment from the conference, Stewart is currently on an indefinite suspension from Beamer. "He came back today and was in the 8 a.m. team meeting we had this morning, and he was at practice," Beamer said. "As I've told him and the team, his status will be determined as we go throughout the week."Stewart was a five-star recruit in the Class of 2024 and one of the most significant recruits of the Beamer era at South Carolina. The junior posted a combined 22.5 tackles for loss and 11 sacks in his first two seasons with the program.
He has yet to record a sack over two games as he works his way back from injury."I do believe my job as the head coach is to win football games, but it's also to help young men and help them grow," Beamer said. "Last week was a learning lesson from him and I (hope) there was growth from that. He's a good young man that I care a lot about. He's not, and I'm not condoning his actions in Tuscaloosa at all, and it's unacceptable, but he's not the first person that has ever punched a player in a game, and he won't be the last."Beamer on the hot seatStewart's return would be a big on-field boost for a South Carolina team in desperate need of one. Beamer entered the season on the hot seat, and that temperature has only increased after three straight losses. Last week's 35-34 overtime defeat to Kentucky was the team's eighth straight in the SEC and 12th setback in its last 14 games against Power Four opponents.Few coaches are facing the amount of pressure that Beamer's under right now, but he doesn't seem worried about his status heading into a Week 6 showdown at Florida.
"It's a challenge. It is what it is. It's week to week in this league and I know that. Right now, 2-3 is not good enough," Beamer said Tuesday. "I haven't been good enough as a head coach. I own it. We've got to get better as a football team. It really doesn't change, going into it versus in it. Right now, I'm focusing on what I can control, and that's trying to put together the best team to go play on Saturdays to give us the best chance to be successful on Saturdays."All I can go on is the conversations I've had with (athletic director) Jeremiah (Donati), (senior deputy director of athletics) Jeff Crane, and the text message I got from our president emeritus over the weekend -- who's been awesome. Some of our biggest donors that I've gotten phone calls, voicemails and text messages … that's why I go on, not what people and their 'sources' say. Then it doesn't happen, and suddenly it's, 'well, my sources now say this. "It's like c'mon man."Recent social media comments about his job on a post centered on his daughter's senior night at her high school, the night before South Carolina's loss to Mississippi State, really bothered Beamer.
"There's some crappy people in the world, there just is," Beamer said, who is currently on a three-week break from checking his phone, he confirmed.CBS Sports reported on Monday that Beamer's job security isn't as tenuous as it seems due to financial constraints at the university.Beamer has mentioned the support he has from the school's administration several times during this current three-game slide and said as much during Tuesday's press conference.
"I don't know if social media is always real-life," Beamer said. "What you see on social media vs. what is actually real. I know the noise out there last week versus what was actually real."The same people in the student section against Mississippi State, chanting 'Fire Beamer' at the end of the game, seven days earlier, they were screaming 'Beamer Ball' at the end of the game when we beat Towson. It's truly week to week."

title: NFL, NFLPA clarify celebration penalties; imitating drinking allowed - CBS Sports
description: Kyle Juszczyk and Jake Ferguson had their fines rescinded Wednesday
body:
Kyle Juszczyk and Jake Ferguson had their fines rescinded Wednesday
        
                                                
                        
                        
    
                                            
                    
                    
                                            
        
    Oct 7, 2026
                            
                    at
    5:20 pm ET
                        
                •
            
            1 min read
            
        
    

            
    
        With several celebration fines -- and fine rescindments -- in the NFL news cycle lately, the league and the NFL Players Association released a joint statement Wednesday "to clarify the line between player expression and conduct that may result in discipline."According to the release, players were reminded that the following could result in a 15-yard unsportsmanlike conduct penalty, a fine or both:Gestures that depict violence, including the use of guns or other weapons, or gang-related signs.Gestures that depict smoking or drug use.Gestures that are sexual in nature.Most notably, the joint statement says "imitating drinking a beverage will not be considered violations or result in discipline."The drinking a beverage celebration had been a topic du jour in the recent days. After Week 2, the NFL fined 49ers fullback Kyle Juszczyk $14,926 for "engaging in an offensive demonstration."Here's the offensive demonstration:
"Your imitation of chugging a beer constituted an offensive demonstration and could reasonably be construed as being in poor taste."However, Juszczyk told ESPN this has always been his celebration, an ode to his nickname "Juice." The NFL reversed the fine Wednesday, hours before the NFL/NFLPA statement.In Week 3, Cowboys tight end Jake Ferguson celebrated a touchdown of his own by pretending to shotgun a beer. The NFL originally fiined him $13,611, but, like Juszczyk, Ferguson explained it was a longtime celebration (of drinking Gatorade) and appealed, and on Wednesday, the fine was rescinded.
Now, players can hydrate to celebrate, no matter their drink of choice.
